```{r}
pick <- function(d, survey_name, disease, indicator_name, sex_name = "All") {
  d[d$survey == survey_name & d$condition == disease & d$indicator == indicator_name &
      d$sex == sex_name, , drop = FALSE]
}

dm15sr <- fmt(pick(t2, "STEPS 2015", "Diabetes", "Self-reported diagnosis"))

htnaware <- fmt(pick(t3, "STEPS 2015", "Hypertension", "Aware among measured disease"))
htntreat <- fmt(pick(t3, "STEPS 2015", "Hypertension", "Treated among measured disease"))
htncontrol <- fmt(pick(t3, "STEPS 2015", "Hypertension", "Controlled among measured disease"))
htn22treat <- fmt(pick(t4, "KDHS 2022", "Hypertension", "Treated among diagnosed"))
htn22insured <- fmt(pick(t4, "KDHS 2022", "Hypertension", "Insured among diagnosed"))
```

# Abstract

**Background**  
Questionnaire surveys measure previously diagnosed non-communicable disease (NCD), whereas examination surveys also detect disease in people who have never been diagnosed. We assessed whether questionnaire-based hypertension and diabetes indicators were comparable across Kenyan surveys and quantified the burden invisible to self-report.

**Methods**  
We analysed nationally representative cross-sectional data from the 2014 Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS), Kenya STEPS 2015, and KDHS 2022. Analyses were restricted to adults aged 18--49 years. Estimates were standardised to the STEPS 2015 sex-by-age distribution and incorporated weights, strata and primary sampling units. We compared self-reported professional diagnosis across surveys, estimated measured disease and care cascades within STEPS, and described treatment and insurance among diagnosed adults in KDHS 2022. Independent-survey differences used Taylor-linearised standard errors. No individual records or cascade stages were combined across surveys.

**Results**  
Standardised self-reported hypertension was `r htn14` in KDHS 2014, `r htn15sr` in STEPS 2015, and `r htn22` in KDHS 2022. The 2014 KDHS--2015 STEPS difference was 0.35 percentage points (95% CI -0.98 to 1.69), supporting comparability of the hypertension self-report item. In STEPS, measured hypertension was `r htn15m`, but only `r htnaware` of affected adults were aware, `r htntreat` were treated, and `r htncontrol` were controlled. Self-reported diabetes varied more across instruments (`r dm14`, `r dm15sr`, and `r dm22`, respectively), while measured diabetes in STEPS was `r dm15m`. In KDHS 2022, `r htn22treat` of diagnosed adults used antihypertensive medication and `r htn22insured` were insured.

**Conclusions**  
Repeated questionnaire surveys consistently captured diagnosed hypertension but represented only a minority of biologically measured hypertension. Questionnaire indicators should therefore monitor contact and diagnosis, not population disease prevalence. Kenya needs surveillance that jointly measures biomarkers, diagnosis, treatment, control and financial protection.

# Background

Hypertension and diabetes are major contributors to cardiovascular and renal disease, yet many affected adults in low- and middle-income countries remain undiagnosed or untreated [@zhou2021global; @geldsetzer2019state; @mannegoehler2016diabetes]. Monitoring this continuum requires distinguishing biological need from health-system contact. A survey that measures blood pressure or glucose can estimate disease regardless of prior contact with care. A questionnaire asking whether a clinician has ever communicated a diagnosis measures a different construct: the cumulative result of access to testing, clinical recognition, and communication to the patient.

Kenya has two complementary national surveillance systems. The World Health Organization STEPwise approach to NCD risk-factor surveillance (STEPS) combines an interview with physical and biochemical measurements [@whoSTEPS; @kenyaSTEPS2015]. The Kenya Demographic and Health Survey (KDHS) collects extensive demographic, service-use and financial-protection information but does not measure adult blood pressure or glucose. Both KDHS 2014 and KDHS 2022 asked adults whether a health professional had told them that they had hypertension or diabetes [@kdhs2014; @kdhs2022]. The 2014 KDHS report explicitly cautioned that these indicators did not estimate biological prevalence because they depended on examination and prior notification [@kdhs2014].

Previous analyses of Kenya STEPS 2015 established a substantial hypertension burden and large losses from diagnosis to control [@mohamed2018prevalence]. Diabetes prevalence, prediabetes and associated factors have also been reported [@mohamed2018diabetes], and a later analysis evaluated modified Finnish diabetes risk scores in the same dataset [@mugume2023findrisc]. Those studies did not formally harmonise questionnaire indicators from the two KDHS rounds with the corresponding STEPS interview items. Consequently, it remains unclear whether differences between DHS self-report and STEPS measurement primarily reflect incompatible questionnaires or the expected visibility gap between diagnosed and measured disease.

We used surveillance triangulation rather than statistical record linkage or data fusion. Our objectives were to: (1) assess the comparability of self-reported hypertension and diabetes diagnosis across KDHS 2014, STEPS 2015 and KDHS 2022 in a common age range; (2) quantify measured disease and losses across the awareness, treatment and control cascade within STEPS 2015; and (3) place KDHS 2022 treatment and insurance indicators among diagnosed adults alongside, but not mathematically combine them with, the measured STEPS burden. The study provides a pre-Social Health Authority baseline for interpreting future questionnaire and biomarker surveillance.

# Methods

## Study design

We conducted a secondary analysis of three nationally representative cross-sectional household surveys. Reporting follows the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology guidance [@vonelm2007strobe]. The unit of analysis was the individual respondent. The surveys sampled different people; no record linkage was possible or attempted.

## Data sources and study population

### KDHS 2014

KDHS 2014 used a stratified, two-stage cluster design based on the national sampling frame. Women aged 15--49 and men aged 15--54 were interviewed. Hypertension and diabetes items asked whether a doctor or health worker had ever told the respondent that they had raised blood pressure/hypertension or raised blood sugar/diabetes [@kdhs2014]. The women's survey used long and short questionnaires; NCD questions were available only in the applicable questionnaire domain. Respondents without an administered NCD item were excluded from that indicator rather than classified as disease-free.

### Kenya STEPS 2015

Kenya STEPS 2015 selected one adult aged 18--69 years per sampled household through a multistage cluster design. Step 1 collected sociodemographic characteristics, risk behaviours and histories of raised blood pressure and glucose. Step 2 included three blood-pressure measurements and anthropometry. Step 3 included fasting capillary glucose and lipids [@kenyaSTEPS2015]. We used the supplied interview, physical-measurement and biochemical weights (`wstep1`, `wstep2`, and `wstep3`) for their corresponding indicators.

### KDHS 2022

KDHS 2022 interviewed women aged 15--49 and men aged 15--54 using a stratified, two-stage design [@kdhs2022]. The NCD module recorded prior professional diagnosis and current medication. Insurance was obtained from the Person Recode variable `sh27` and linked to women and men through cluster, household and household-line identifiers. As in 2014, women outside the administered NCD questionnaire domain were excluded, not coded as negative.

For direct comparability, all analyses were restricted to women and men aged 18--49 years. This avoids the unequal female and male upper-age limits in DHS and the substantially older STEPS population.

## Indicators

Self-reported hypertension and diabetes diagnosis were defined in each survey as having ever been told by a doctor or other health worker that the respondent had the condition. In STEPS, systolic and diastolic pressure were the means of the second and third readings. Measured hypertension was systolic pressure at least 140 mmHg, diastolic pressure at least 90 mmHg, or reported use of blood-pressure medication during the preceding two weeks. Measured diabetes was fasting capillary glucose at least 7.0 mmol/L or current glucose-lowering medication.

Among adults with measured hypertension, awareness was previous professional diagnosis or medication use; treatment was medication use during the preceding two weeks; and control was treatment with systolic pressure below 140 mmHg and diastolic pressure below 90 mmHg. Analogous awareness and medication indicators were calculated for measured diabetes, although diabetes estimates were treated as secondary because of the small numerator.

In KDHS 2022, treatment was current medication among respondents reporting the corresponding diagnosis. Insurance was any coverage (`sh27`) among diagnosed respondents. These indicators retain diagnosed adults as their denominator and were not rescaled to measured disease using information from another survey.

## Standardisation and statistical analysis

Each survey was analysed separately using its sampling weights, primary sampling units and strata. We formed six standardisation cells from sex and age (women and men, each aged 18--29, 30--39 and 40--49). Estimates were directly standardised to the weighted distribution of these cells in the STEPS 2015 interview sample. The standard distribution was treated as fixed and applied to all three surveys. This made pooled estimates comparable without ad hoc multiplication of male and female survey weights.

Percentages are presented with 95% confidence intervals from Taylor-linearised variances. Differences between independent survey estimates used the square root of the sum of their variances. We treated the near-contemporaneous KDHS 2014--STEPS 2015 comparison of identically worded self-report constructs as an assessment of instrument-level convergence. The measured-versus-aware comparison within STEPS quantified the surveillance visibility gap directly in the same respondents. We did not interpret differences between STEPS 2015 and KDHS 2022 as biological disease trends.

Analyses were conducted in R using `survey`, `haven` and `data.table`. The complete workflow is implemented in `03_scripts/06_triangulation_analysis.R`; tables and figures are generated programmatically.

## Ethical considerations

The original surveys obtained national ethical approvals and participant consent. This study used de-identified secondary data under authorised DHS and STEPS access. No participant contact occurred. Planned dissemination will follow the data custodians' acknowledgement and publication-review requirements.

# Results

## Questionnaire domains and analytic samples

The harmonised NCD domains contained 23,199 KDHS 2014 respondents, 3,527 STEPS respondents with a non-missing hypertension self-report item, and 26,487 KDHS 2022 respondents aged 18--49. The smaller female DHS domains reflect assignment of the NCD questions to the applicable questionnaire, not outcome non-response (Supplementary Table S1). Treating those structurally missing records as negative would have substantially underestimated diagnosed disease.

## Convergence of self-reported diagnosis indicators

Age-sex-standardised self-reported hypertension was `r htn14` in KDHS 2014, `r htn15sr` in STEPS 2015, and `r htn22` in KDHS 2022 (Table 1; Figure 1). KDHS 2014 exceeded STEPS 2015 by only 0.35 percentage points (95% CI -0.98 to 1.69). The KDHS 2022 estimate was 0.58 percentage points lower than KDHS 2014 (95% CI -1.20 to 0.05), providing little evidence of a material change in diagnosed hypertension prevalence after standardisation.

Women consistently reported more diagnosed hypertension than men. Estimates for women were 10.0%, 9.4%, and 8.9% in KDHS 2014, STEPS 2015 and KDHS 2022, respectively; corresponding estimates for men were 3.3%, 3.2%, and 3.3%. This stable sex contrast across three independent samples supports reproducibility of the questionnaire indicator while also reflecting sex differences in screening, care contact, true disease, or all three.

Self-reported diabetes was `r dm14` in KDHS 2014, `r dm15sr` in STEPS 2015, and `r dm22` in KDHS 2022 (Table 2). KDHS 2014 exceeded STEPS 2015 by 0.58 percentage points (95% CI 0.24 to 0.92). Thus the hypertension items converged more closely than the diabetes items.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-self-report
#| tbl-cap: "Age-sex-standardised self-reported hypertension diagnosis among Kenyan adults aged 18-49 years"
show <- t2[t2$condition == "Hypertension", c("survey", "sex", "formatted", "n", "events")]
names(show) <- c("Survey", "Sex", "% (95% CI)", "n", "Events")
knitr::kable(show, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-self-report-dm
#| tbl-cap: "Age-sex-standardised self-reported diabetes diagnosis among Kenyan adults aged 18-49 years"
show <- t2[t2$condition == "Diabetes", c("survey", "sex", "formatted", "n", "events")]
names(show) <- c("Survey", "Sex", "% (95% CI)", "n", "Events")
knitr::kable(show, align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## Measured disease and care cascades in STEPS 2015

Measured hypertension prevalence in adults aged 18--49 was `r htn15m`, approximately three times the contemporaneous STEPS self-reported diagnosis prevalence (Table 3). Among adults with measured hypertension, `r htnaware` were aware, `r htntreat` were taking medication, and `r htncontrol` were treated and controlled. Expressed across the full population, 3.8% had aware hypertension, 1.2% had treated hypertension, and 0.6% had controlled hypertension.

Measured diabetes prevalence was `r dm15m`. Awareness and treatment among the 59 unweighted measured cases were 9.6% and 8.9%, respectively, with wide confidence intervals. These estimates should be interpreted cautiously because a single fasting capillary measurement is a surveillance definition rather than a clinical diagnosis and because the number of measured cases was small.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-steps-cascade
#| tbl-cap: "Measured disease and care-cascade indicators in Kenya STEPS 2015, ages 18-49"
show <- t3[t3$sex == "All", c("condition", "indicator", "formatted", "n", "events")]
show$indicator <- c("HTN measured", "HTN aware among cases",
                    "HTN treated among cases", "HTN controlled among cases",
                    "HTN aware population", "HTN treated population",
                    "HTN controlled population", "Diabetes measured",
                    "Diabetes aware among cases", "Diabetes treated among cases")
show <- show[, c("indicator", "formatted", "n", "events")]
names(show) <- c("Indicator", "Estimate", "N", "Cases")
knitr::kable(show, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## Treatment and insurance among diagnosed adults in KDHS 2022

Among adults reporting diagnosed hypertension in KDHS 2022, `r htn22treat` reported current medication and `r htn22insured` had any health insurance (Table 4). Diagnosed and treated hypertension represented 1.9% of the standardised adult population. Among respondents reporting diagnosed diabetes, 59.8% were treated and 37.0% were insured, although the diagnosed diabetes domain was much smaller.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-kdhs-care
#| tbl-cap: "Treatment and insurance among adults with self-reported diagnosis in KDHS 2022, ages 18-49"
show <- t4[t4$sex == "All", c("condition", "indicator", "formatted", "n", "events")]
show$indicator <- c("HTN treatment", "HTN insurance", "HTN treated prevalence",
                    "Diabetes treatment", "Diabetes insurance", "Diabetes treated prevalence")
show <- show[, c("indicator", "formatted", "n", "events")]
names(show) <- c("Indicator", "Estimate", "N", "Cases")
knitr::kable(show, align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"), row.names = FALSE)
```

# Discussion

## Principal findings

Three findings emerge. First, questionnaire-based hypertension diagnosis was highly reproducible across KDHS 2014, STEPS 2015 and KDHS 2022 after restricting the surveys to the same ages and applying a common sex-by-age standard. The close 2014--2015 agreement indicates that the large difference between questionnaire diagnosis and measured hypertension cannot be dismissed as a DHS-versus-STEPS wording artefact.

Second, questionnaire surveillance saw only the diagnosed portion of the burden. In STEPS, approximately one in five adults aged 18--49 met the surveillance definition for hypertension, but fewer than one in five of those affected were aware and only about one in eighteen were treated. The policy denominator therefore matters. Treatment among people already diagnosed describes continuity of care after detection; it does not describe effective coverage among everyone needing treatment.

Third, the repeated DHS indicator did not show convincing improvement in diagnosed hypertension prevalence between 2014 and 2022. A stable diagnosis proportion cannot distinguish stable disease burden from simultaneous changes in disease incidence and detection. It should not be read as evidence that hypertension prevalence was unchanged. The consistent female--male contrast may reflect both biological differences and women's greater contact with health services, particularly through reproductive and maternal care.

## Relation to previous research

The hypertension cascade observed here is directionally consistent with the previously published all-age Kenya STEPS analysis, which reported high prevalence and low awareness, treatment and control [@mohamed2018prevalence]. Our estimates differ because we restricted the population to ages 18--49, directly standardised all surveys to one distribution, and used the medication item associated with the physical-measurement module. The purpose was comparability with DHS rather than replacement of the official all-age estimate.

International pooled analyses have shown that hypertension and diabetes cascades lose patients at each step, with particularly poor diagnosis and control in sub-Saharan Africa [@geldsetzer2019state; @mannegoehler2016diabetes]. Those analyses harmonised surveys that contained biomarkers and care indicators in the same respondents. Our findings show why cascade stages should not be multiplied across independent surveys when the age ranges, years and instruments differ. Triangulation is more defensible when each source retains its own estimand and agreement is assessed on genuinely shared indicators.

The diabetes findings deserve greater caution. The difference between KDHS 2014 and STEPS 2015 self-report suggests weaker cross-instrument comparability, while the measured diabetes numerator was small. A prior Kenya analysis evaluated FINDRISC using the same STEPS data [@mugume2023findrisc]. Our study does not derive another risk score; it instead demonstrates that diabetes surveillance conclusions are more sensitive than hypertension conclusions to instrument and sampling choices.

## Implications for surveillance and policy

Kenya's transition from the National Health Insurance Fund to the Social Health Authority creates a need for indicators spanning need, contact, quality and financial protection. DHS can monitor diagnosis, treatment among diagnosed people and insurance. It cannot determine how many adults have undiagnosed hypertension or diabetes without biomarkers. Conversely, STEPS measures biological risk but contains less detail about financing and service use.

Future national surveillance should place blood pressure, glucose, prior diagnosis, medication, control and insurance in the same respondents. At minimum, a periodic STEPS round should include insurance and care-access modules, or a future KDHS biomarker subsample should measure adult blood pressure and glucose. Until then, dashboards should present measured prevalence from examination surveys and diagnosed-adult indicators from questionnaire surveys side by side, with explicit denominators and survey years.

The low treatment coverage among measured hypertension indicates that insurance expansion alone is insufficient. Screening must be connected to confirmatory diagnosis, reliable medicine supply, longitudinal follow-up and control monitoring. The male awareness deficit warrants screening routes beyond routine facility attendance, including workplaces, community outreach and opportunistic blood-pressure measurement.

## Strengths and limitations

This study used three national probability samples, preserved each complex survey design, enforced a common age range, standardised estimates to one sex-by-age distribution and explicitly respected questionnaire domains. The near-contemporaneous KDHS 2014--STEPS 2015 comparison separated instrument convergence from the measured-versus-self-report gap. All outputs are generated through a reproducible R workflow.

Several limitations remain. First, the surveys are repeated cross-sections rather than a cohort; individual transitions between cascade stages cannot be observed. Second, only the 2015 survey measured biomarkers, so biological changes through 2022 cannot be estimated. Third, blood pressure and glucose measured on one survey occasion are surveillance classifications and may misclassify clinical disease. Fourth, self-report depends on recall, access and clinician communication. Fifth, diabetes case numbers in STEPS were small. Sixth, the standard population was estimated from STEPS and treated as fixed, so uncertainty in the standardisation distribution was not propagated. Finally, treatment and insurance in KDHS 2022 apply only to diagnosed adults and cannot identify treatment or financial protection among all adults with biological disease.

# Conclusions

Self-reported hypertension diagnosis was consistent across three Kenyan national surveys when age, sex and questionnaire domains were harmonised. That consistency strengthens the interpretation of the larger STEPS measured-versus-aware gap: questionnaire-only surveillance reliably describes known disease but misses most adults with hypertension. Diabetes comparisons were less stable and require more cautious interpretation. Kenya should not use DHS diagnosis prevalence as a substitute for measured NCD prevalence, nor combine cascade stages from different surveys as if they came from one population. Integrated biomarker, care and insurance measurement is necessary to monitor effective NCD coverage during the Social Health Authority era.
